628	                                           detrimental effects on the subsequent night of sleep. Consequently, due to the potential diffi-
629	                                           culties to increase sleep acutely in the context of team sport, practitioners should consider
630	                                           keeping consistent sleep patterns and potentially add a post lunch nap during the day follow-
631	                                           ing a late exercise if a decrease in total sleep time is observed. Several studies have highlighted
632	                                           that when sleep restriction occurs, napping could be an efficient strategy to maintain total
633	                                           sleep time [1] but also performance [34, 35]. However, guidance regarding nap timing (e.g.
634	                                           between 13:00 to 16:00) and duration (e.g. <30min) need to be provided to the athletes [31].
635	                                           Moreover, the increase in fragmentation index, as well WASO was observed, suggesting that
636	                                           sleep was more disturbed in SE and may lead to restless sleep. Those results suggest that sleep
637	                                           quality should be improved concurrently to the sleep extension protocol. The importance of
638	                                           improving sleep quality is further reinforced by recent findings showing that collision activity
639	                                           could deteriorate sleep architecture [36].
640	
641	
642	                                           The effects of sleep extension and active recovery on recovery at POST 14
643	                                           The main results showed that SE affected cognitive function positively, although there was no
644	                                           improvement in recovery status of the lower body neuromuscular function at POST 14. Simi-
645	                                           larly, Fullagar et al. [9] found that an acute sleep hygiene strategy did not improve physical
646	                                           recovery after a football match. They hypothesised that neuromuscular function failed to
647	                                           improve because difference in terms of sleep quantity (i.e. total sleep time) was not sufficient
648	                                           (�1h). However, in the current study the effective difference in total sleep time between
649	                                           groups was much larger (� 02h30), but still did not result in any improvement in lower body
650	                                           neuromuscular function. This suggests that recovery of neuromuscular function following
651	                                           training and collision exposure is not sensitive to acute changes in total sleep time.
652	                                               The difference in cognitive function between groups in the current study is not surprising.
653	                                           It is well documented that sleep restriction has deleterious consequences for cognitive function
654	                                           [37]. The CON group’s total sleep time was low (� 04h30) which likely caused the large
655	                                           between group difference. Despite the absence of a substantial between group difference, HRR
656	                                           took longer to recover in the SE group. This suggests that the active recovery protocol may
657	                                           have had a positive effect on HRR by potentially improve parasympathetic activation [38].
658	                                           However, further research is required to show this conclusively.
659	                                               The mechanisms underpinning the differences between cognitive and physical recovery
660	                                           remain hypothetical. It has been shown that restricting sleep towards the end of the night
661	                                           reduces the proportion of Rapid Eye Movement (REM) while Non-REM (NREM) was con-
662	                                           served [39]. Those adjustments could explained the present results as NREM has been linked
663	                                           to cellular repair and energy storing while REM aims to improve cognitive processes [40]. In
664	                                           this study, the inclusion of an early morning session would have resulted in a reduction of
665	                                           REM proportion and therefore could explain the lack of difference on neuromuscular function
666	                                           as this suggests that the proportion of NREM was similar in both groups. However, results
667	                                           regarding professional football players showed that players went to bed later (i.e. �02:00 AM)
668	                                           than the present bedtime (i.e. midnight) observed in this study. While this is a realistic
669	                                           assumption, further research needs to explore the effect of different sleep restriction scenarios
670	                                           (morning vs. evening sleep restriction) and their respective effects on post-exercise recovery.
671	                                               Nevertheless, it is possible that a more targeted approach to enhance NREM could improve
672	                                           neuromuscular recovery as total sleep time did not seem to affect recovery positively or nega-
673	                                           tively. This necessity to improve NREM post-exercise is further strengthened by recent find-
674	                                           ings showing that the contact activity sustained during match may specifically decrease NREM
675	                                           [36]. Further research is required to understand how sleep extension may change sleep archi-
676	                                           tecture and consequently post-recovery kinetics.

685	                                           The effects of sleep extension and active recovery at POST 36
686	                                           While observing residual fatigue 30 hours following contact-based activity is normal [41], the

                                           Discussion
                                           The aim of this study was to assess the effect of one night of sleep extension on recovery kinet-
                                           ics compared to an active recovery session prescribed early in the morning. The main finding
                                           of this study was that at 14h post training (POST 14), sleep extension resulted in improved
                                           cognitive performance, while active recovery resulted in improved upper body neuromuscular
                                           and autonomic function. However, at 36h post training (POST 36) no substantial differences
                                           between conditions were present. These findings suggest that the effects of acute recovery
                                           interventions are in themselves acute, and that recovery interventions will have varied effects
                                           on the diverse aspects of recovery during this acute period. Consequently, if athletes must per-
                                           form again within short timeframes (e.g. multi days event, congested fixtures), practitioners
                                           can consider which recovery protocols that best align to the performance requirements. In
                                           cases where longer recovery is possible, it remains unknown if a sleep extension performed
                                           over several days would be more beneficial than active recovery.

                                           Standardized training session and acute responses
                                           The results of the current study suggest that the standardised training session induced imme-
                                           diate (i.e. POST 0) and substantial changes in perceptual fatigue measures, neuromuscular
                                           function and HRR. Neither cognitive nor upper body neuromuscular parameters were affected
                                           by the training exposure at POST 0. The decreases in perceptual fatigue and lower body neuro-
                                           muscular function were persistent at POST 14 and POST 36. Roe et al. [16] reported similar
                                           results regarding perceptual recovery despite different responses regarding the neuromuscular
                                           function. While Roe et al. [16] observed a change in upper body neuromuscular function, in
                                           the present study, only lower body neuromuscular function was affected. The reason for this
                                           difference remains hypothetical but could be related to the player level (academy vs. univer-
                                           sity). No between group differences were observed at POST 0 for any measure indicating that
                                           the training exposure caused similar fatigue effects in both conditions. Collectively, these
                                           results suggest that the standardized training session is a reliable protocol to induce substantial
                                           fatigue responses over two days and could be used for future research.

                                           The effects of sleep extension and active recovery on sleep parameters at
                                           night 1
                                           During night 1, the SE intervention elicited a very large increase in the time spent in bed and
                                           consequently total sleep time in comparison to CON. However, while time in bed improved,
                                           total sleep time only demonstrated a small improvement compared to baseline (� 1 hour)
                                           reaching only the 7h of total sleep time which is line with recommendation for healthy individ-
                                           ual [30] but potentially below what is recommended and needed for athletes [31, 32]. In a simi-
                                           lar study [9], participants increased total sleep time only by 1h after a football match played in
                                           the evening (i.e. match finished at 22:30). These results suggest that it is difficult to acutely
                                           extend total sleep time by more than 1h in team sport athletes. This may be because the rapid
                                           change in sleep schedule conflicts with established circadian rhythms [33]. While in this study,
                                           participants slept in their home environment, in practical settings, elite athletes often slept in
                                           different environment could also limits the integration of sleep extension for this population.
                                           Furthermore, poorer sleep on Night 2 (i.e. shorter total sleep time, increased Fragmentation
                                           Index and WASO) for the SE group suggesting that sleep extension may have some

                                           detrimental effects on the subsequent night of sleep. Consequently, due to the potential diffi-
                                           culties to increase sleep acutely in the context of team sport, practitioners should consider
                                           keeping consistent sleep patterns and potentially add a post lunch nap during the day follow-
                                           ing a late exercise if a decrease in total sleep time is observed. Several studies have highlighted
                                           that when sleep restriction occurs, napping could be an efficient strategy to maintain total
                                           sleep time [1] but also performance [34, 35]. However, guidance regarding nap timing (e.g.
                                           between 13:00 to 16:00) and duration (e.g. <30min) need to be provided to the athletes [31].
                                           Moreover, the increase in fragmentation index, as well WASO was observed, suggesting that
                                           sleep was more disturbed in SE and may lead to restless sleep. Those results suggest that sleep
                                           quality should be improved concurrently to the sleep extension protocol. The importance of
                                           improving sleep quality is further reinforced by recent findings showing that collision activity
                                           could deteriorate sleep architecture [36].


                                           The effects of sleep extension and active recovery on recovery at POST 14
                                           The main results showed that SE affected cognitive function positively, although there was no
                                           improvement in recovery status of the lower body neuromuscular function at POST 14. Simi-
                                           larly, Fullagar et al. [9] found that an acute sleep hygiene strategy did not improve physical

                                           neuromuscular function. This suggests that recovery of neuromuscular function following
                                           training and collision exposure is not sensitive to acute changes in total sleep time.

          The Effect of Body Mass on Eccentric Knee-Flexor Strength
           Assessed With an Instrumented Nordic Hamstring Device
                         (Nordbord) in Football Players
                                Martin Buchheit, Yannick Cholley, Mark Nagel, and Nicholas Poulos

      Purpose: To exam ine the effect o f body mass (BM ) on eccentric knee-flexor strength using the N ordbord and offer sim ple guide­
      lines to control for the effect of BM on knee-flexor strength. Methods: D ata from 8 1 soccer players (U 1 7 ,U 1 9 ,U 2 1 , senior 4th
      French division, and professionals) and 41 A ustralian Football League (AFL) players w ere used for analysis. They all perform ed
      1 set o f 3 m axim al repetitions o f the bilateral N ordic ham string exercise, with the greatest strength m easure used for analysis.
      The m ain regression equation obtained from the overall sam ple was used to predict eccentric knee-flexor strength from a given
      BM (m oderate TEE, 22% ). Individual deviations from the B M -predicted score w ere used as a BM -free index o f eccentric knee-
      flexor strength. Results: T here was a large (r = .55, 90% confidence lim its .42;.64) correlation betw een eccentric knee-flexor
      strength and BM. H eavier and older players (professionals, 4th French division, and A FL) outperform ed their lighter and younger
      (U 1 7 -U 21) counterparts, with the soccer professionals presenting the highest absolute strength. Professional soccer players were
      the only ones to show strength values likely slightly greater than those expected for their BM. Conclusions: E ccentric knee-
      flexor strength, as assessed w ith the N ordbord, is largely BM -dependent. To control for this effect, practitioners may com pare
      actual test perform ances with the expected strength for a given BM , using the follow ing predictive equation: Eccentric strength
      (N) = 4 x BM (kg) + 26.1. Professional soccer players w ith specific knee-flexor-training history and enhanced neurom uscular
      perform ance may show higher than expected values.

 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Cross-sectional Study",
 "primaryDomain":"Monitoring & Technology",
 "domains":["Monitoring & Technology","Sports Medicine & Injury"],
 "audiences":["Performance","Athletic Training","Research & Analytics"],
 "sports":["Soccer","Other Sport"],
 "populations":["Youth / Adolescent","Professional / Elite"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Cross-sectional analysis of single-visit Nordbord eccentric knee-flexor testing in 122 football players: 81 soccer players (U17, U19, U21 academy, 4th French division, and professional) and 41 Australian Football League players, all tested in season. Eccentric strength correlated largely with body mass (r = 0.55, 90% CI 0.42 to 0.64) and was not materially changed by adjustment for body fat. The authors report the regression equation eccentric strength (N) = 4 x body mass (kg) + 26.1, and that only the professional soccer players were likely slightly (about 20%) stronger than their body-mass-expected values.",
 "screeningLimitations":"Data were collected as routine in-season monitoring in six squads, with one test visit per player and no injury outcomes, so the equation describes strength differences but cannot show that body-mass adjustment predicts injury risk. Sex is not stated in the text, and the regression is specific to these groups.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the body-mass equation as a validated injury threshold, when the study only quantifies how test scores vary with body mass and gives no injury data.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2016,
   "citation":"Buchheit M, Cholley Y, Nagel M, Poulos N. The Effect of Body Mass on Eccentric Knee-Flexor Strength Assessed With an Instrumented Nordic Hamstring Device (Nordbord) in Football Players. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2016;11(6):721-726.",
   "doi":"10.1123/ijspp.2015-0513",
   "abstract":"Data from 81 soccer players (youth academy, 4th French division and professional) and 41 AFL players were used to examine how body mass affects eccentric knee-flexor strength measured with the Nordbord. Eccentric strength correlated largely with body mass, and the authors offer a regression equation to compare individual test results with body-mass-expected values.",
   "tldr":"Nordbord eccentric hamstring strength rises with body mass, so a single absolute threshold may misclassify heavier and lighter players. Practitioners can compare an athlete's score with the body-mass-expected value from the reported equation.",
   "methods":"Single-visit Nordbord testing (one set of three maximal Nordic hamstring repetitions, average of both legs) in 122 players from six groups, collected in season as routine monitoring. Body mass, skinfolds and percentage body fat were measured. Linear regression, log-transformed data, allometric scaling and magnitude-based inference were used. Players with an injury in the prior six months were excluded.",
   "findings":"Across all players, eccentric knee-flexor strength correlated largely with body mass (r = 0.55, 90% CI 0.42 to 0.64); adjusting for body fat did not change the correlation. The regression equation is eccentric strength (N) = 4 x body mass (kg) + 26.1, with a typical error of about 22% (65 N). Absolute strength was highest in the professional soccer group (411 +/- 65 N), and only the professional soccer players were likely slightly (about 20%) stronger than their body-mass-expected values.",
   "limitations":"This was a cross-sectional analysis of one test visit per player, so it cannot show test-retest change or injury prediction. Data came from six groups with different ages, standards and training histories, and the allometric exponent varied between them (0.57 to 1.51). Sex is not stated in the text. Individual differences smaller than about 40 N (12%) could not be reliably judged in a single test.",
   "practicalImplications":"When comparing players of different body mass, or tracking one player whose body mass changes, staff can compare the Nordbord score with the body-mass-expected value from the reported equation. A single absolute strength threshold without body-mass adjustment may be misleading. The study gives no data on whether the adjusted values predict injury.",
   "athleteDev":"Use the body-mass-expected Nordbord value to judge whether an individual's eccentric knee-flexor strength is below or above expectation. Differences under about 40 N (12%) in a single test should not be read as meaningful. Regular retesting would give stronger evidence of change.",
   "rtp":"This study cannot be used to judge return to sport or set clearance criteria. It contains no injured-player or post-injury data, and it excludes players with recent injury."
 }
}

ABSTRACT: To investigate the effect of 20 min nap opportunity (N20), 5 mg · kg-1 of caffeine (CAF) and their            Tarak Driss
combination (CAF+N20) on the biochemical response (energetic biomarkers, biomarkers of muscle damage                    0000-0001-6109-7393
and enzymatic antioxidants) to the running-based anaerobic sprint test. Fourteen highly trained male athletes
                                                                                                                        Karim Chamari
completed in a double-blind, counterbalanced and randomized order four test sessions: no nap with placebo               0000-0001-9178-7678
(PLA), N20, CAF and CAF+N20. Compared to PLA, all treatments enhanced maximum and mean powers.
Minimum power was higher [(mean difference) 58.6 (95% confidence interval = 1.31–116) Watts] after CAF                  Omar Hammouda
                                                                                                                        0000-0002-5002-687x
and [102 (29.9–175) Watts] after CAF+N20 compared to N20. Also, plasma glucose was higher after
CAF [0.81 (0.18–1.45) mmol · l-1] and CAF+N20 [1.03 (0.39–1.64) mmol · l-1] compared to N20. However, plasma
lactate was higher [1.64 (0.23–3.03) mmol · l-1] only after N20 compared to pre-exercise, suggesting a higher
anaerobic glycolysis during N20 compared to PLA, CAF and CAF+N20. Caffeine ingestion increased post-
exercise creatine kinase with [54.3 (16.7–91.1) IU · l-1] or without napping [58.9 (21.3–96.5) IU · l-1] compared
to PLA. However, superoxide dismutase was higher after napping with [339 (123–554) U · gHB-1] or without
caffeine [410 (195–625) U · gHB-1] compared to PLA. Probably because of the higher aerobic glycolysis contribution
in energy synthesis, caffeine ingestion resulted in better repeated sprint performance during CAF and CAF+N20
sessions compared to N20 and PLA. Caffeine ingestion resulted in higher muscle damage, and the short nap
enhanced antioxidant defence with or without caffeine ingestion.

   "abstract":"Seventy-five elite young male football academy players were screened radiologically for femoroacetabular impingement and followed for six seasons.    "tldr":"In one elite academy, young male football players with cam or pincer hip morphology had a higher rate of hamstring injury than players without it. Recurrence and time to return were higher too, but these differences were not statistically significant.",
   "methods":"Prospective data collection with retrospective analysis over six seasons in 75 elite young male academy players from one club. Hip morphology was assessed on pelvic radiographs at pre-season or pre-transfer examinations using alpha angle, lateral centre-edge angle and Tonnis angle criteria. Non-contact hamstring injuries, their treatment durations and recurrences were recorded. Chi-square and independent-samples t-tests were used, with P < 0.05 as significant.",
   "findings":"The hamstring injury rate was higher in players with cam and/or pincer morphology (14 of 23, 60.9%) than without (18 of 52, 34.6%; p = 0.034). Morphology players were older (20.35 vs 18.92 years) and heavier (71.5 vs 67.7 kg), and these differences were significant.",
   "limitations":"The morphology group was small (n = 23) and the two groups differed in age and body weight, which were not adjusted for. The Results text gives 60.09% for injury in the morphology group, but 14 of 23 is 60.9%, which matches Table 2. Figure 1 treatment durations are not significant.",
   "practicalImplications":"Screening for cam and pincer morphology could help identify young football players who may have a higher hamstring injury rate, so staff may want to monitor them more closely.    "rtp":"The study reports time to return after hamstring injury, but the difference was not significant and the sample was small. It cannot set return-to-play criteria or show that morphology should change clearance timing."

873	                                           p � .05, �� p � .01, ��� p � .001.
874	                                           https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0279109.g007
875	
876	                                           hot, compared to a temperate, environment. There was partial support for our first hypothesis
877	                                           (H1), whereby soccer-specific decision-making scores (calculated in line with a panel of
878	                                           experts’ decisions) was impaired in 32˚C compared to 18˚C. However, no condition × time
879	                                           effects were observed for decision-making scores which was not aligned to our hypotheses. As
880	                                           expected, intermittent sprint performance was impaired in the second half compared to the
881	                                           first half of the CISP in 32˚C, but did not deteriorate in 18˚C. In support of the second hypoth-
882	                                           esis (H2), ‘future planning’ verbalisations were significantly lower in 32˚C compared to 18˚C,
883	                                           and more responses categorised as ‘lack of evaluation’ were observed in the second half com-
884	                                           pared to the first half across conditions. This partly reflected lower-level thought processing in
885	                                           the hot condition and following a half of intermittent sprint activity, which partially affirmed
886	                                           our second hypothesis (H2). However, we did not find condition × time interactions as origi-
887	                                           nally anticipated. We also found support for our third hypotheses (H3), whereby players had a
888	                                           heightened threat state and felt more unpleasant in 32˚C compared to 18˚C. Moreover, MET
889	                                           and NMET concentration were significantly higher following exercise, and these increases
890	                                           were greater in the hot compared to the temperate condition, which reflected a heightened
891	                                           physiological stress response when exercising in hot condition thereby supporting our fourth
892	                                           hypothesis (H4). It is worth noting that these findings were similar when analysing data with 8
893	                                           participants when conditions were fully counterbalanced, and a summary of these findings can
894	                                           be found in the supporting information.
895	
896	
897	                                           Heat on cognitive performance
898	                                           It was anticipated that a more pronounced decline in decision-making score would be
899	                                           observed during the CISP in the hot condition compared to the temperate condition due to
900	                                           additional physiological stress experienced (i.e., higher HR; greater fluid loss; higher TC during
901	                                           latter stages of each half of the CISP) [22,29,31]. Decision-making score was found to be lower
902	                                           throughout all time-points in the hot compared to the temperate condition, but no interaction
903	                                           effect was observed. Resting decision-making was assessed once participants had entered the
904	                                           chamber, and it is possible that passive exposure to hot conditions may have contributed to
905	                                           reducing decision-making performance. Indeed, research has noted that an alteration in sub-
906	                                           jective state during a short period of passive heat exposure has been shown to impair complex
907	                                           cognitive function [58]. From an occupational perspective, a review by Moda, Filho & Minhas
908	                                           [59] found that increased ambient temperature reduced vigilance levels in outdoor workers,
909	
910	
911	
912	PLOS ONE | https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0279109 December 15, 2022                                                                           17 / 24
913	 PLOS ONE                                                        Exercise-induced fatigue and heat on soccer-specific decision-making during exercise
914	
915	
916	
917	                                           which increased the risk of lapses in safety measures. Previous research has proposed that a TC
918	                                           threshold of ~38.5˚C is where cognitive function becomes impaired [60]. However, these find-
919	                                           ings suggest that when using more situation, or sport, specific complex decision-making tasks,
920	                                           this threshold may be less sparing where TC did not exceed this threshold in the majority of
921	                                           participants.
922	                                              A ‘think-aloud’ protocol was also implemented, recording participants retrospective evalua-
923	                                           tion of each situation to understand what factors were being considered when making the
924	                                           decision, and if this was affected by exercise-induced fatigue or heat stress. Interestingly, the-
925	                                           matic analysis revealed that participants verbalised significantly less ‘future planning’ evalua-
926	                                           tions when in the hot compared to the temperate condition. These findings align with
927	                                           previous research, which found that within 15-min of passive heat exposure (50˚C, 30%rh)
928	                                           complex planning performance is significantly impaired [58]. This decline was attributed to
929	                                           the alliesthesial effect [61], where immediate sensory displeasure and negative affective states
930	                                           induced by a rapid elevation in skin temperature were thought to contribute to the cognitive
931	                                           impairments observed [58]. Heat exposure can be considered an interfering cognitive load,
932	                                           placing further demands on the limited cognitive workspace and thus reducing the availability
933	                                           of neural resources for use in more complex cognitive tasks [58,62].
934	                                              Verbalisations referencing tactical awareness and execution difficulty were also significantly
935	                                           lower in the second half compared to the first half of the CISP. Additionally, statements which
936	                                           lacked evaluation were higher in the second half compared to the first half, and reference to
937	                                           specific player movement were also significantly reduced in the second half in the hot condi-
938	                                           tion. Support can be drawn from Casanova et al. [27], who found that fatigue induced by pro-
939	                                           longed high-intensity intermittent exercise resulted in more impulsive decisions underpinned
940	                                           by lower-level thought processes being observed toward the end of the first half and second
941	                                           half, compared to the beginning of the first half. These findings also align with the transient
942	                                           hypofrontality hypothesis which explains that during physically demanding activity, neural
943	                                           resources are diverted toward regions of the brain responsible for maintaining motor func-
944	                                           tions, limiting the availability of resources for the pre-frontal cortex to engage in higher-order
945	                                           thought processing [20]. Although it should be acknowledged that the extent of the differences
946	                                           concerning decision-making evaluation in the present research should be taken with some
947	                                           caution given the number of analyses conducted for the range of themes extracted, these find-
948	                                           ings suggest that players’ ability to engage in higher level thought processes may be reduced in
949	                                           hot conditions due to an even greater demand for resources in the primary motor cortex dur-
950	                                           ing more strenuous conditions.
951	                                              Another possible explanation is that the heat stress in the present research could have also
952	                                           potentially induced some anxiety (as partially suggested by the negative affective states and
953	                                           higher threat state) that may have contributed in reducing soccer players’ focus during the
954	                                           decision-making task. For example, based on the premises of the Integrated Model of Anxiety
955	                                           and Perceptual-Motor Performance [63] anxiety can reduce focus on task-relevant cues and
956	                                           increase the likelihood of being distracted by task-irrelevant stimuli, and thereby possibly
957	                                           impaired the depth of decision-making in the heat. Future research could consider assessing
958	                                           specific emotions such as anxiety, rather than affective states, to test such possibilities. Addi-
959	                                           tionally, the environmental heat stress may have contributed to a heightened demand for
960	                                           resources to process current events (i.e., maintaining power output and making the immediate
961	                                           decision), reducing athletes’ ability to predict and plan. This supports that fatigue induced by
962	                                           prolonged high-intensity intermittent exercise may result in athletes making decisions based
963	                                           on lower-level thought-processing [27], and that heat exposure may also impair higher-level
964	                                           appraisal of dynamic situations as they occur.
965	
966	
967	
968	
969	PLOS ONE | https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0279109 December 15, 2022                                                                    18 / 24
970	 PLOS ONE                                                        Exercise-induced fatigue and heat on soccer-specific decision-making during exercise
971	
972	
973	
974	                                           Heat on physical performance, appraisal, affect and metanephrines
975	                                           Heat also impaired athletes’ physical performance in this study. Power output was significantly
976	                                           lower during the second half compared to the first half in the hot condition (-~7%) but was
977	                                           not different between halves in the temperate condition. Previous research has shown that
978	                                           increased perceived exertion and more negative affective states induced by heat exposure can
979	                                           impair self-paced work rate [64]. Moreover, intermittent sprint performance is shown to be
980	                                           adversely affected by heat exposure, when marked hyperthermia is experienced (i.e., TC
981	                                           >39˚C) [65]. However, in this study, TC reached values lower than those typically expected
982	                                           when performing team sport in the heat (>~39˚C) [65]. This was perhaps due to the inclusion
983	                                           of a cycling-based protocol, as metabolic heat production experienced during running based
984	                                           activity tends to be higher [66].
985	                                               The present research also observed higher NMET and MET levels (measured as the more
986	                                           stable metabolites of norepinephrine and epinephrine) at half-time and post- exercise com-
987	                                           pared to pre-exercise, but such increases were to a much greater extent in the hot compared to
988	                                           temperate condition. This aligns with previous research that has observed that the release of
989	                                           epinephrine and norepinephrine is accelerated in response to acute heat stress [29]. The
990	                                           increased HR, fluid loss, RPE, thermal sensation as well as heightened threat and more
991	                                           unpleasant affective states, also observed in the heat, support that participants were under
992	                                           additional physiological and perceptual strain in the hot condition, despite TC reaching aver-
993	                                           age heights of ~38.4˚C. It is suggested that when players feel their TC increasing more rapidly
994	                                           in hot conditions, they may deliberately or reflexively reduce their high-intensity work to
995	                                           reduce the rate of metabolic heat production and ensure thermal strain does not exceed tolera-
996	                                           ble limits [67]. In this study, unpleasant affective states were exacerbated toward the end of
997	                                           each half in the hot condition, which may have driven the reduction in work output observed
998	                                           from the outset of the second half. Core temperature was higher at the end of the first half
999	                                           compared to the second half in the hot condition, supporting that reducing high-intensity
1000	                                           work reduced the levels of thermal strain experienced in the second half. This may also explain
1001	                                           why decision-making performance did not decline more markedly in the second half in 32˚C.
1002	                                           Nonetheless, such responses appear to support a heightened physiological and possibly psy-
1003	                                           chological stress response in hot compared to temperate conditions.
1004	                                               The present study also identified that participants’ demand appraisals were higher and
1005	                                           resource appraisals were lower in hot condition compared to the temperate condition, reflec-
1006	                                           tive of an overall higher threat state in the hot compared to the temperate condition. Naturally,
1007	                                           when performing in hot environments, individuals are likely to perceive that higher effort may
1008	                                           be required than in temperate conditions due to the widely understood exacerbated physiolog-
1009	                                           ical responses (i.e., TC, HR sweat rate and dehydration) [22]. Furthermore, as competing in
1010	                                           hot environments is uncommon for the sample in this study, some uncertainty as to how they
1011	                                           would cope could be expected due to a lack of experience and knowledge in performing in
1012	                                           these environments, which may have contributed to the heightened threat state observed [28].
1013	                                           Based on the premises of the TCTSA [28], threat states are argued to be linked with more
1014	                                           unpleasant affective states, and impaired cognitive functioning (e.g., decision-making, concen-
1015	                                           tration) and performance. Therefore, it is possible that heat exposure induced a higher threat
1016	                                           state, which may have contributed to accounting for the more unpleasant affective states,
1017	                                           impaired decision-making, and lowered physical work output, in the hot condition compared
1018	                                           to the temperate condition in the present research. Although such causal inferences are beyond
1019	                                           the scope of this research, further research may wish to consider directly testing this
1020	                                           possibility.
1021	
1022	
1023	
1024	
1025	PLOS ONE | https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0279109 December 15, 2022                                                                    19 / 24
1026	 PLOS ONE                                                        Exercise-induced fatigue and heat on soccer-specific decision-making during exercise
1027	
1028	
1029	
1030	                                           Limitations and future research
1031	                                           Whilst this study built upon previous methods by integrating a sport-specific visual decision-
1032	                                           making task, research should incorporate tasks which require simultaneous visual and audi-
1033	                                           tory attention (e.g., dual-task paradigms) to better replicate the demands of match-play. Addi-
1034	                                           tionally, a cycling intermittent sprint protocol was used to allow players to modulate their own
1035	                                           high-intensity physical work output as per match-play, whilst simultaneously investigating
1036	                                           cognitive function and central mechanisms. Despite this being widely employed within team
1037	                                           sport literature [39,40], it is probable that physiological stress would have been more noticeable
1038	                                           during running-based activity [66]. This would better replicate the demands of match-play
1039	                                           and it is plausible that further cognitive decrements may be observed during running-based
1040	                                           activity. Also, the premises of the TCTSA [28] is that challenge and threats states rely upon
1041	                                           motivated performance. Conducting testing in a laboratory setting may have limited motiva-
1042	                                           tion compared to “real-world” competitive match-play. However, it could be assumed that
1043	                                           these athletes were motivated due to them being well trained volunteer soccer players, and
1044	                                           effort was incentivised through promotion of some level of competition simulated through the
1045	                                           inclusion of a cash prize. Nevertheless, we do not know the extent that participants were moti-
1046	                                           vated, nor understand the type of motivation they had, during the task. Therefore, researchers
1047	                                           may wish to consider addressing such considerations in future studies to further enhance the
1048	                                           external validity of our findings. It should also be noted that metabolites of noradrenaline and
1049	                                           adrenaline were measured in this study, providing insights into MET and NMET activation
1050	                                           during exercise in the heat. Researchers may also wish to measure cortisol and adrenocortico-
1051	                                           tropic hormone to assess PAC activation [e.g., 28] and provide deeper insights about neuroen-
1052	                                           docrinal response to exercise in the heat.
1053	
1054	                                           Conclusions
1055	                                           In this research, soccer-specific decision-making was impaired in the hot compared to temper-
1056	                                           ate condition. Physical work output was also significantly reduced in the second half in the
1057	                                           heat but was not affected in the temperate condition. These decrements were observed when
1058	                                           TC was �38.5˚C, suggesting that complex, situation-specific decision-making as well as physi-
1059	                                           cal work output can be impaired below TC thresholds proposed previously when exposed to

                                           latter stages of each half of the CISP) [22,29,31]. Decision-making score was found to be lower
                                           throughout all time-points in the hot compared to the temperate condition, but no interaction
                                           effect was observed. Resting decision-making was assessed once participants had entered the
                                           chamber, and it is possible that passive exposure to hot conditions may have contributed to
                                           reducing decision-making performance. Indeed, research has noted that an alteration in sub-
                                           jective state during a short period of passive heat exposure has been shown to impair complex
                                           cognitive function [58]. From an occupational perspective, a review by Moda, Filho & Minhas
                                           [59] found that increased ambient temperature reduced vigilance levels in outdoor workers,



PLOS ONE | https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0279109 December 15, 2022                                                                           17 / 24
 PLOS ONE                                                        Exercise-induced fatigue and heat on soccer-specific decision-making during exercise



                                           which increased the risk of lapses in safety measures. Previous research has proposed that a TC
                                           threshold of ~38.5˚C is where cognitive function becomes impaired [60]. However, these find-
                                           ings suggest that when using more situation, or sport, specific complex decision-making tasks,
                                           this threshold may be less sparing where TC did not exceed this threshold in the majority of
                                           participants.
                                              A ‘think-aloud’ protocol was also implemented, recording participants retrospective evalua-
                                           tion of each situation to understand what factors were being considered when making the
                                           decision, and if this was affected by exercise-induced fatigue or heat stress. Interestingly, the-
                                           matic analysis revealed that participants verbalised significantly less ‘future planning’ evalua-
                                           tions when in the hot compared to the temperate condition. These findings align with
                                           previous research, which found that within 15-min of passive heat exposure (50˚C, 30%rh)
                                           complex planning performance is significantly impaired [58]. This decline was attributed to
                                           the alliesthesial effect [61], where immediate sensory displeasure and negative affective states
                                           induced by a rapid elevation in skin temperature were thought to contribute to the cognitive
                                           impairments observed [58]. Heat exposure can be considered an interfering cognitive load,
                                           placing further demands on the limited cognitive workspace and thus reducing the availability
                                           of neural resources for use in more complex cognitive tasks [58,62].
                                              Verbalisations referencing tactical awareness and execution difficulty were also significantly
                                           lower in the second half compared to the first half of the CISP. Additionally, statements which
                                           lacked evaluation were higher in the second half compared to the first half, and reference to
                                           specific player movement were also significantly reduced in the second half in the hot condi-
                                           tion. Support can be drawn from Casanova et al. [27], who found that fatigue induced by pro-
                                           longed high-intensity intermittent exercise resulted in more impulsive decisions underpinned
                                           by lower-level thought processes being observed toward the end of the first half and second
                                           half, compared to the beginning of the first half. These findings also align with the transient
                                           hypofrontality hypothesis which explains that during physically demanding activity, neural
                                           resources are diverted toward regions of the brain responsible for maintaining motor func-
                                           tions, limiting the availability of resources for the pre-frontal cortex to engage in higher-order
                                           thought processing [20]. Although it should be acknowledged that the extent of the differences
                                           concerning decision-making evaluation in the present research should be taken with some
                                           caution given the number of analyses conducted for the range of themes extracted, these find-
                                           ings suggest that players’ ability to engage in higher level thought processes may be reduced in
                                           hot conditions due to an even greater demand for resources in the primary motor cortex dur-
                                           ing more strenuous conditions.
                                              Another possible explanation is that the heat stress in the present research could have also
                                           potentially induced some anxiety (as partially suggested by the negative affective states and
                                           higher threat state) that may have contributed in reducing soccer players’ focus during the
                                           decision-making task. For example, based on the premises of the Integrated Model of Anxiety
                                           and Perceptual-Motor Performance [63] anxiety can reduce focus on task-relevant cues and
                                           increase the likelihood of being distracted by task-irrelevant stimuli, and thereby possibly
                                           impaired the depth of decision-making in the heat. Future research could consider assessing
                                           specific emotions such as anxiety, rather than affective states, to test such possibilities. Addi-
                                           tionally, the environmental heat stress may have contributed to a heightened demand for
                                           resources to process current events (i.e., maintaining power output and making the immediate
                                           decision), reducing athletes’ ability to predict and plan. This supports that fatigue induced by
                                           prolonged high-intensity intermittent exercise may result in athletes making decisions based
                                           on lower-level thought-processing [27], and that heat exposure may also impair higher-level
                                           appraisal of dynamic situations as they occur.

 PLOS ONE                                                        Exercise-induced fatigue and heat on soccer-specific decision-making during exercise



                                           Heat on physical performance, appraisal, affect and metanephrines
                                           Heat also impaired athletes’ physical performance in this study. Power output was significantly
                                           lower during the second half compared to the first half in the hot condition (-~7%) but was
                                           not different between halves in the temperate condition. Previous research has shown that
                                           increased perceived exertion and more negative affective states induced by heat exposure can
                                           impair self-paced work rate [64]. Moreover, intermittent sprint performance is shown to be
                                           adversely affected by heat exposure, when marked hyperthermia is experienced (i.e., TC
                                           >39˚C) [65]. However, in this study, TC reached values lower than those typically expected
                                           when performing team sport in the heat (>~39˚C) [65]. This was perhaps due to the inclusion
                                           of a cycling-based protocol, as metabolic heat production experienced during running based
                                           activity tends to be higher [66].
                                               The present research also observed higher NMET and MET levels (measured as the more
                                           stable metabolites of norepinephrine and epinephrine) at half-time and post- exercise com-
                                           pared to pre-exercise, but such increases were to a much greater extent in the hot compared to
                                           temperate condition. This aligns with previous research that has observed that the release of
                                           epinephrine and norepinephrine is accelerated in response to acute heat stress [29]. The
                                           increased HR, fluid loss, RPE, thermal sensation as well as heightened threat and more
                                           unpleasant affective states, also observed in the heat, support that participants were under
                                           additional physiological and perceptual strain in the hot condition, despite TC reaching aver-
                                           age heights of ~38.4˚C. It is suggested that when players feel their TC increasing more rapidly
                                           in hot conditions, they may deliberately or reflexively reduce their high-intensity work to
                                           reduce the rate of metabolic heat production and ensure thermal strain does not exceed tolera-
                                           ble limits [67]. In this study, unpleasant affective states were exacerbated toward the end of
                                           each half in the hot condition, which may have driven the reduction in work output observed
                                           from the outset of the second half. Core temperature was higher at the end of the first half
                                           compared to the second half in the hot condition, supporting that reducing high-intensity
                                           work reduced the levels of thermal strain experienced in the second half. This may also explain
                                           why decision-making performance did not decline more markedly in the second half in 32˚C.
                                           Nonetheless, such responses appear to support a heightened physiological and possibly psy-
                                           chological stress response in hot compared to temperate conditions.
                                               The present study also identified that participants’ demand appraisals were higher and
                                           resource appraisals were lower in hot condition compared to the temperate condition, reflec-
                                           tive of an overall higher threat state in the hot compared to the temperate condition. Naturally,
                                           when performing in hot environments, individuals are likely to perceive that higher effort may
                                           be required than in temperate conditions due to the widely understood exacerbated physiolog-
                                           ical responses (i.e., TC, HR sweat rate and dehydration) [22]. Furthermore, as competing in
                                           hot environments is uncommon for the sample in this study, some uncertainty as to how they
                                           would cope could be expected due to a lack of experience and knowledge in performing in
                                           these environments, which may have contributed to the heightened threat state observed [28].
                                           Based on the premises of the TCTSA [28], threat states are argued to be linked with more
                                           unpleasant affective states, and impaired cognitive functioning (e.g., decision-making, concen-
                                           tration) and performance. Therefore, it is possible that heat exposure induced a higher threat
                                           state, which may have contributed to accounting for the more unpleasant affective states,
                                           impaired decision-making, and lowered physical work output, in the hot condition compared
                                           to the temperate condition in the present research. Although such causal inferences are beyond
                                           the scope of this research, further research may wish to consider directly testing this
                                           possibility.

content.text: Q62's key numbers and limitations are in hand. The study was a laboratory crossover, planned for 10 players but stopped early at 9, and the counterbalancing was incomplete. I'll write the draft with those limits stated.

92	Soccer is the largest and most popular sport in the world (Lovett, 2018). Crucial to the
93	outcome of a soccer match is the ability to score goals. The soccer kick has been
94	extensively studied as a crucial element in this regard (Barfield et al., 2002). Two
95	important components of a well-performed kick are ball speed and the accuracy with
96	which a player is able to place the ball (Dörge et al., 2002; Katis et al., 2013; Lees & Nolan,
97	1998). The ability to achieve high speed and accuracy in soccer kicks may be influenced
98	by muscle fatigue as the physical demands of soccer are characterised by intermittent
99	high-intensity work (Bangsbo, 2014; Bangsbo et al., 2006). This intermittent work leads
100	to both momentary fatigue during a match due to high-intensity periods as well as
101	gradual accumulation of fatigue towards the end of the game (Dambroz et al., 2022).

108	with their consent.

112	   Muscle fatigue is defined by Allen, Lamb referred to as prolonged low frequency
113	force depression or low-frequency fatigue (LFF). LFF is a phenomenon charac­
114	terised by a greater decrease in muscle force production when tested at low
115	stimulation frequencies compared to high stimulation frequencies after fatiguing
116	muscle contractions (Keeton & Binder-Macleod, 2006). Furthermore, recovery of
117	muscle performance is slow from LFF, and typically ranges from a few hours to
118	several days (De Ruiter et al., 2005; Edwards et al., 1977; Jones et al., 1989). The
119	primary cause of LFF is a reduced release of Ca++ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
120	(Allen et al., 2008). In humans LFF elicits deficits in both force and power during
121	dynamic contraction (Herskind et al., 2023). In a soccer context, LFF has been
122	demonstrated to be present during post-match recovery expressed as reduced 10 hz/
123	100 hz muscle stimulation force ratio (Rampinini et al., 2011). Although fatigue of
124	more temporary character is also present after intense periods during soccer
125	matches (Mohr et al., 2005) we have focussed particularly on the more long-
126	lasting LFF in the present study.
127	   In experiments based on multi-joint movements, Forestier and Nougier (1998) exam­
128	ined the effect of muscle fatigue in the wrist flexor muscles on coordination and accuracy
129	of seated throwing. Fatigue, induced by isometric contractions of the wrist flexor,
130	reduced the proportion of accurate throws from 77% to 57%. This reduced accuracy
131	occurred concomitantly with changes in throwing mechanics from a successive prox­
132	imal-to-distal accelerating movement to a more simultaneous movement of joint systems
133	(shoulder, elbow, and wrist) displaying increased rigidity (Forestier & Nougier, 1998).
134	These results are interesting in a soccer context as soccer kicks in a fresh state follow
135	similar movement characteristics as throwing (Kellis & Katis, 2007). Whether changing
136	kinematics due to fatigue are also present during a maximal soccer kick is uncertain.
137	   The literature on soccer kicks indicates that maximal kick speed and foot speed before
138	ball contact are reduced in the fatigued state immediately after intense activity

140	2006; Torreblanca-Martínez et al., 2020). However, due to lack of objective assessments
141	of muscle fatigue, the level of fatigue among the participants in these studies is uncertain.

576	study appears to occur simultaneously with a numerical decrease in maximum foot speed
577	just before ball contact.
578	   In our study it is assumed that the decrease in maximum foot speed during the kick
579	explains the decrease in maximum ball speed. This is supported by the fact that the ball
580	speed/foot speed ratio did not significantly change on the intervention day compared to
581	the control day (−0,011 CI= [−0,086;0,064] p = 0.75). The results are based on the
582	maximal trial from the participants and therefore limit the conclusions to successful
583	trials in fatigued state.
584	   The present study utilised direct measures of decline in muscle performance (torque)
585	when investigating the effect of muscle fatigue on kicking accuracy. Many studies do not
586	measure muscle performance directly before and after a fatigue protocol and therefore do
587	not know whether or to what degree the participants are fatigued during the following
588	tests of kicking performance (Bjelica et al., 2013; R. Ferraz et al., 2017; Kellis et al., 2006;
589	Russell et al., 2011; W. Young et al., 2010). However, Torreblanca-Martínez et al. (2020)
590	did use direct measures of fatigue (decrease in sprint performance) and found a 5.67%
591	reduction on ball speed and a non-significant decrease in kicking accuracy of 7.69%.
592	 14      J. B. CARSTENSEN ET AL.
593	
594	
595	Despite a numerical decrease in players’ kicking accuracy, no significant results are found
596	due to large variation compared to ball speed (Katis et al., 2013; Radman, Wessner, Bachl,
597	Ruzic, Hackl, Prpic, et al., 2016). These findings are similar to the results of the present
598	study. However, Torreblanca-Martínez et al. (2020) did not include a control group for
599	comparison of kicking performance. Hence, limiting the possibility to detect the true
600	effect of the fatigue protocol as the none-fatigued condition could differ from a no-
601	change effect. This is supported by the findings of the present study and Currell et al.
602	(2009) who found a significant improvement in shooting performance in their interven­
603	tion compared with placebo. The present study showed an improvement in kicking
604	accuracy on the control day of 13.3% (p = 0.02). Despite this conclusion, the significant
605	improvement observed on the control day still comes as a surprise to us and is to our
606	knowledge not observed before perhaps due to the lack of control conditions in many
607	studies. Given the high level among the study participants, the standardised warm-up
608	protocol, and the uncomplicated test protocol, we did not anticipate any change on the
609	control day. Nevertheless, this unexpected outcome occurred hence, demonstrating the
610	importance of including a control group in tests where an effect over time is not expected.
611	   In studies by Ferraz et al. (2019) and Russell et al. (2011) a combination of direct and
612	indirect measures of muscle fatigue was used. Analogous to our study, the studies do not
613	find decreases in kicking accuracy. The studies used a decrease in running performance,
614	heart rate, and perceived exertion on the Borg scale. The results from these studies show
615	that heart rate and perceived fatigue increase, while the direct measures (running
616	performance) do not change (R. M. P. Ferraz et al., 2019; Russell et al., 2011).
617	Therefore, it is uncertain whether the participants actually experienced muscle fatigue
618	in these studies, which could potentially explain why kicking accuracy was not affected.
619	   The distribution of kicks from the participants in the accuracy test was described using
620	bivariate normal distribution and showed similar characteristics to the results from
621	Hunter et al. (2018). Accordingly, the effect of the fatiguing muscle contractions was
622	an increased short axis on the error ellipse describing the distribution of the kicks. This is
623	thought to be due to a disturbance in the timing of muscle activation in the kicking
624	motion caused by the effect of fatigue on contractile properties in the involved muscu­
625	lature. When kicking a rolling ball this disturbance in timing may have resulted in
626	a larger variance in the distance between support leg placement and ball in the moment
627	of contact with the kicking leg.
628	
629	
630	Role of the quadriceps muscle
631	The type of fatigue that we have induced in the present study, LFF, seems to primarily
632	decrease the muscle’s ability to develop force during slow or static contractions
633	without the same diminishing effect on maximum contraction velocity (Herskind,
634	2022; Herskind et al., 2022). This influence on the force-velocity curve of muscles
635	exposed to LFF possibly affects intersegmental coordination during complex multi-
636	joint movements like the instep kick. However, it should be noted that there is limited
637	data on the effect of LFF on muscle contractions near maximum contraction velocity,
638	and conclusions based on these data should be cautious (Herskind, 2022). Therefore,
639	if the force velocity relationship of the m. quadriceps is affected during fatigue kicking
640	conditions reducing timing of muscle activation and intersegmental coordination this
641	                                                               SPORTS BIOMECHANICS      15
642	
643	
644	would cause a reduction in maximal foot- and ball speed as observed in the present
645	study.

due to large variation compared to ball speed (Katis et al., 2013; Radman, Wessner, Bachl,
Ruzic, Hackl, Prpic, et al., 2016). These findings are similar to the results of the present
study. However, Torreblanca-Martínez et al. (2020) did not include a control group for

indirect measures of muscle fatigue was used. Analogous to our study, the studies do not

decrease the muscle’s ability to develop force during slow or static contractions
without the same diminishing effect on maximum contraction velocity (Herskind,
2022; Herskind et al., 2022). This influence on the force-velocity curve of muscles
exposed to LFF possibly affects intersegmental coordination during complex multi-
joint movements like the instep kick. However, it should be noted that there is limited
data on the effect of LFF on muscle contractions near maximum contraction velocity,

if the force velocity relationship of the m. quadriceps is affected during fatigue kicking
conditions reducing timing of muscle activation and intersegmental coordination this

Conclusion
The findings of the present study showed a reduction in the players’ maximum kicking
speed following a fatigue inducing protocol of the quadriceps femoris muscle. A decrease

 "studyDesign":"Randomized Controlled Trial",
 "primaryDomain":"Recovery & Readiness",
 "domains":["Recovery & Readiness","Athlete Wellbeing"],

 "sports":["Rugby"],
 "populations":["Male Athletes","Collegiate"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Randomised single-blind crossover study of 10 male university rugby union players (12 recruited, 2 removed for poor sleep-protocol compliance). After a late evening training session, players either extended time in bed to about 10 hours or attended an early morning (07:30) active recovery session, across three weeks. Sleep extension increased time in bed and total sleep time versus control on the first night, but also increased sleep fragmentation; at 14 h post-training, cognitive (Stroop) recovery was faster with sleep extension, while HR recovery and upper-body neuromuscular function were better with active recovery; no between-group difference in recovery status was seen at 36 h.",
 "screeningLimitations":"Ten players in one squad, with a single standardised session and actigraphy-only sleep measurement, limit generalisation. Between-group differences were reported as unclear or small for most outcomes, and the authors note baseline sleep was below recommended levels.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the cognitive benefit at 14 h as evidence that acute sleep extension improves recovery overall, when lower-body neuromuscular and 36 h recovery showed no clear between-group benefit.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2022,
   "citation":"Leduc C, Weaving D, Owen C, et al. The effect of acute sleep extension vs active recovery on post exercise recovery kinetics in rugby union players. PLoS ONE. 2022;17(8):e0273026.",
   "doi":"10.1371/journal.pone.0273026",
   "abstract":"Ten male university rugby union players completed a randomised single-blind crossover study comparing one night of sleep extension (time in bed up to 10 hours) with an early morning active recovery session after a late standardised training session. Physical, perceptual and cognitive recovery were measured before, immediately after, 14 h and 36 h after training.",
   "tldr":"A single night of sleep extension after late training improved cognitive recovery at 14 h in university rugby players, but did not improve lower-body neuromuscular recovery, and made sleep more fragmented. Recovery status at 36 h did not differ between sleep extension and an early morning recovery session.",
   "methods":"Randomised single-blind crossover over three weeks with 10 male university rugby players. Each week, players completed a standardised 19:30 full-contact session, then either extended sleep or attended a 07:30 active recovery session (15 min bike and 15 min mobility). Wristwatch actigraphy, a wellness questionnaire, a computerised Stroop test, heart rate recovery, running load index, countermovement jump and plyometric push-up were measured. Linear mixed models with effect sizes and magnitude-based decisions were used.",
   "findings":"Sleep extension increased time in bed (very large vs control, first night) and total sleep time (most likely, first night, sleep extension about 2 h 30 min more than control), but also produced greater sleep fragmentation than control (between-group effect 2.85 [2.00 to 3.70]). At 14 h, Stroop completion time was most likely shorter with sleep extension (between-group effect -1.53 [-2.33 to -0.74]), while heart rate recovery was likely better with active recovery (-1.00 [-1.85 to -0.16]). Within-group changes in countermovement jump power were most likely reduced from 0 h to 36 h in both conditions. No between-group difference in recovery status was observed at 36 h.",
   "limitations":"Twelve players were recruited but only 10 were analysed, and the study was in one squad. Actigraphy cannot measure sleep stages. Baseline sleep was below the recommended 7-9 hours, so a sleep debt may have masked effects. Chronotype was mid-range for all players and could not be analysed. Most between-group outcomes were unclear, and the effects that did reach significance were few.",

   "abstract":"Twenty-five healthy participants performed running, drop jumping and 180-degree change-of-direction movements barefoot, with fresh ankle tape, and after 15 minutes of sports-specific use.    "tldr":"Fresh ankle taping reduced peak ankle inversion during running, jumping and change-of-direction movements in healthy adults. Most ACL and overuse risk measures did not rise, but peak loading rate did increase, and some effects were still present after 15 minutes of use.",
   "methods":"Randomised repeated-measures design with barefoot (BF), fresh tape (TF) and tape after 15 minutes of sports-specific use (TU) conditions, with sex as a between-subject factor. Twenty-five healthy participants (10 women, 15 men) performed drop jumps from 25 cm, running at 4.5 m/s and 180-degree change of direction at 3.0 m/s on a force platform, with three valid trials per movement and condition. Kinematics were recorded by 22 cameras at 200 Hz and kinetics by two force platforms at 1000 Hz. Standard taping was applied by one sports physician. Participants ran, accelerated, changed direction and jumped in their own sports shoes for 15 minutes between TF and TU data collection.",
   "findings":"Fresh tape and tape after sports-specific use significantly reduced peak ankle inversion. Ankle dorsiflexion was significantly restricted by taping during change of direction and running, and the fresh-tape effect on some variables differed between women and men.",
   "limitations":"Participants were healthy and not athletes, and no athletes with chronic ankle instability were tested. Only one taping method was used, and the study was done in a lab with barefoot conditions, which the authors note does not reflect shod use in sport.    "practicalImplications":"Fresh ankle taping can reduce peak ankle inversion during sports movements in healthy players, which is the mechanism linked to sprain risk. The effects after 15 minutes of use were mixed, so taping should not be assumed to protect equally throughout a session.",
   "athleteDev":"Taping may reduce ankle inversion during running, landing and cutting, with little change to most knee and hip risk measures. Staff should watch loading rate and overuse symptoms, since the ground reaction force loading rate increased.",
   "rtp":"This study cannot be used to set return-to-play decisions. It tested healthy participants with no injuries and did not include athletes with chronic ankle instability or recent sprains."
 }
}
